newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters resume talks, but differences remain.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters resume talks, but differences remain.

text.p: United Parcel Service on Monday continued its marathon talks with the Teamsters union as the bargaining approached a make-or-break moment that could resolve the 15-day-old strike or escalate it.
UPS Chairman James Kelly said the company and the Teamsters were closer to settling the strike, but predicted it could go "much, much longer" if negotiations were to break off this week.
The strike by 185,000 Teamsters has crippled the nation's largest carrier of small packages, costing UPS $650 million so far while strikers scrape by on strike benefits of $55 a week.
"We are indeed closer than we were four days ago, but there are still some very difficult issues for them (negotiators) to discuss today," Kelly told Cable News Network.
Teamsters spokesman Steve Trossman was noncommittal about the prospects for a deal but agreed the talks were reaching a critical point.

"The reality is we could reach agreement today and we may not reach agreement today," he told reporters. "Yes, if we don't conclude negotiations through these discussions this week, it certainly could go on for much, much longer."
The two sides began talks Thursday at the request of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman. The talks continued with only brief breaks for sleep until late Sunday night, when they adjourned for 12 hours.
But with both sides facing the prospect of digging in for the long haul if the strike is not quickly settled, the company and the union were poised to escalate their campaigns.

The UPS board will discuss hiring replacement workers at a board meeting Wednesday, spokesman Norman Black said. In an interview with CNN, Kelly did not deny the possibility such replacements were under consideration.
"The last thing we want to do is replace them, but the longer it goes the more options we have to consider," he said of the company's striking workers.
Black said no decision had been made to hire replacement workers "and this company is loathe to take that approach."

At the same time, the Teamsters sought to broaden their base of support. It announced news conferences by a coalition of women's groups and activist religious groups to talk about the issue of part-time work. The union has made demands for more full-time jobs central to its dispute with UPS.
The union also planned to pass out leaflets at retail stores, accusing them of offering the same kinds of part-time, lower-paying jobs that the Teamsters dislike at UPS.

Pointedly, the Teamsters targeted companies -- such as Kmart, Toys R Us, Circuit City and Home Depot -- which were among retailers who wrote President Clinton asking that he seek an injunction to halt the strike.
White House spokesman Barry Toiv sounded a slightly more cautious note Monday about the chances of solving the dispute than President Clinton had expressed on Sunday.

Clinton "is still hopeful they will reach a settlement and he continues to urge the parties to work hard to bridge their remaining differences," Toiv told reporters on Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts where the president is vacationing.
On Sunday, Clinton has said it was his "gut feeling" that UPS and the Teamsters would settle. "They're that close," he said, holding up two fingers not very far apart.
The strike is the largest in the United States since a three-day 1976 strike by 400,000 Teamster truck drivers, according to Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd.
